summary: Maine has a transfer rule, but it points at the buyer rather than the seller: anyone who buys or takes a single-family home or multiapartment building by sale or exchange must sign and date a certification at closing promising to install smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors, and must actually install them within 30 days of acquiring or moving in, if they are not already there.
alarmType: For the transfer rule, smoke detectors must be installed per the manufacturer's instructions and may be powered by the building's electrical service or by battery. CO detectors installed under the transfer rule must be powered both by the building's electrical service and by a battery, and go in each area within, or giving access to, bedrooms. Maine's general smoke detector rules (which apply by construction date, not by sale) require detectors in single-family homes finished after January 1, 1982, in each multifamily unit, and in additions or conversions completed after September 19, 1985; any smoke detector installed or replaced within 20 feet of a kitchen or of a bathroom with a tub or shower must be photoelectric, though ionization detectors are still allowed inside bedrooms. Detectors must be listed by a nationally recognized independent testing laboratory. 10-year sealed tamper-resistant battery detectors are expressly allowed for a landlord in a single-family rental.
coAlarms: Treated in a separate statute but with the same transfer rule: a buyer of a single-family dwelling or multiapartment building after October 31, 2009 must certify at closing and install CO detectors within 30 days if none are present, powered by both electrical service and battery, in each area within or giving access to bedrooms. Outside of sale, CO detectors are required in each multifamily unit, in certain group and children's facilities, in licensed hotels, motels, inns and bed and breakfasts, in additions that add a bedroom, in conversions, and in newly built single-family homes.
certification: No fire department inspection and no seller affidavit. The purchaser signs and dates a certification at closing that they will install the detectors properly. Violating either transfer provision is a civil violation with a fine of up to $500, which a court may waive if the problem is fixed within 10 days of a complaint. The statutes also say outright that violating the transfer rule does not create a defect in title, and they bar damage claims over detector performance against the owner, the purchaser, their agents, a closing agent or a lender.
citation: 25 M.R.S. § 2464(10) (smoke detectors, transfer of dwelling); 25 M.R.S. § 2468(6) (carbon monoxide detectors, transfer of dwelling)
lastAmended: 2009 for the smoke detector section (PL 2009, c. 551); 2017 for the carbon monoxide section (PL 2017, c. 322)
notVerified: No one verifies compliance. Because the duty falls on the buyer after closing and the statute says a violation is not a title defect, there is nothing in the law that stops a sale from closing if detectors are missing - this is weaker in practice than a fire-department-certificate state.

The Department of Public Safety rules on smoke and CO detectors, which 25 M.R.S. §§ 2464(4-A) and 2468(7) direct the Commissioner to adopt and which cover approved devices and installation details, were not read. Those rules may add specifics not in the statute.

Whether a newly built or substantially renovated home must meet stricter requirements under the Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code was not checked; the transfer provisions themselves set only the minimum described above.

25 M.R.S. § 2468 was read but its printed SECTION HISTORY list was not captured in full, so 2017 (PL 2017, c. 322) is the latest amendment seen in the text of the subsections, not a confirmed last-amended date for the whole section.
Statute text was read on legislature.maine.gov, which states the page data was extracted on 10/05/2026; changes from any 2026 session after that date were not checked.
